ref: Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Romans 4:1
note: The commentary imagines a person under pressure yielding something precious; Ignatius asks that beasts grind him like God's wheat so he may become Christ's pure bread, giving martyrdom the shape of painful production.

Ignatius calls the shared Eucharist medicine of immortality and an antidote to death; this Christian interpretation turns the commentary's medicinal image toward communal nourishment and rescue from death.

basis: Steadfast work is not in vain
note: Paul calls the community steadfast and abundant in the Lord's work, assuring them that their labor is not empty; this counters the commentary's language of human loss with enduring good action.

basis: Tested faith compared with refined gold
note: Peter says tested faith, more precious than perishable gold refined by fire, will result in praise and honor; this gives pressure a refining yield, though by fire rather than squeezing.

The commentary describes pressure drawing out an essence of worth; Peter says tested faith is more precious than perishable gold refined by fire, using another physical ordeal to explain enduring value.
Peter asks what credit there is in enduring punishment for wrongdoing, then calls it grace to endure suffering while doing good; this tightly joins patient endurance to righteous action.

The commentary couples good action and patience under pressure; Peter distinguishes punishment for wrongdoing from enduring suffering while doing good, so moral value depends on what the pressured person does.

basis: Admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
note: Paul urges the church to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this combines mutual moral care with patience in concrete cases.

The surah closes with believers counseling one another in patience; Paul directs the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient toward all, putting counsel and endurance in the same set of relations.

basis: Seek the good of one another and everyone
note: The church must not repay evil for evil but always pursue good for one another and all; this connects reciprocal ethical counsel to doing good.
The commentary's valuable result of pressure is shared goodness; Paul says comfort received from God in affliction equips sufferers to comfort others, making the product of distress transferable.
The commentary treats the hard-won essence as goodness given to others; Paul says his affliction serves the community's comfort and salvation, effective as they patiently endure the same sufferings.

basis: outer person wastes, inner person renews
note: The commentary places the diminished human beside a preserved inner good; Paul says the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed daily, specifying what can endure inside the fragile vessel of 4:7.

The commentary says pressure may yield a valuable result beyond the loss it inflicts; Paul says momentary affliction produces an eternal weight of glory, continuing the account of pressed but uncrushed people in 4:8.

Paul places treasure in fragile earthen vessels; this gives a close vessel image for the commentary's bottled essence, while locating the value in the vessel's contents rather than in a bitter remedy.

The commentary places diminished humanity between valuable contents and a holding vessel; Paul describes treasure carried in clay jars so the extraordinary power belongs to God rather than to the fragile holders.
Paul says the community is pressed yet not crushed; this directly answers the commentary's image of the human as squeezed matter that decreases, with pressure failing to exhaust the people.

The commentary develops pressure on the human as a possible route to saving essence; Paul says the afflicted are pressed on every side but are not crushed, making the difference between pressure and final loss explicit.
Paul distinguishes being struck down from being destroyed; this counters the commentary's equation of human pressure with decrease by describing survival after blows.

basis: God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness
note: Paul uses seed, bread, and an increased harvest of righteousness; this connects agricultural yield to the commentary's good essence and gives generosity an ethical harvest image.
Paul says the community is enriched in every way for generosity; this closely matches the commentary's report that expressed juice serves as a figure for goodness and giving.

The commentary's container matters because it keeps something useful; Paul says a cleansed vessel is set apart and ready for every good work, moving from a vessel's condition to the person's capacity for beneficial action.

basis: The Lord's servant must be patient and able to teach
note: Paul describes the Lord's servant as not quarrelsome but patient and able to teach; this joins patient conduct to truthful instruction, though it is pastoral rather than reciprocal.

basis: Correct opponents gently toward knowledge of truth
note: The servant is to correct opponents gently in hope that God grants them knowledge of truth; this directly joins correction and truth, adding a one-directional teaching scene to the commentary's mutual counsel.

basis: Correct, rebuke, and exhort with patience and teaching
note: Paul charges Timothy to preach, correct, and exhort with patience and teaching; unlike the commentary's mutual practice, this is a ministerial instruction, but it joins truth-directed correction to patience.

The surah joins giving counsel and sabr; Timothy is instructed to correct, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching, making endurance a quality of the counsel itself, though the instruction is addressed to one teacher.

basis: life poured out as drink offering
note: The commentary's extracted liquid represents the value produced under pressure; Paul, nearing death, describes himself as already being poured out as a drink offering, turning personal loss into an offered gift.

basis: Put on patience with other virtues
note: Paul tells the community to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience; this places patience among shared ethical dispositions, extending the commentary's community defined by sabr.

basis: Bear with and forgive one another
note: The addressees are told to bear with and forgive one another; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel in patience a concrete practice of forbearance.

basis: Teach and admonish one another with the word
note: Paul tells the community to teach and admonish one another with wisdom as Christ's word dwells among them; this is a close communal counterpart to mutual counsel in truth.
Paul immediately says believers are created in Christ for good works; this keeps the contrast from erasing action and offers a distinct account of deeds as the intended result of salvation.

basis: Salvation as a gift through faith
note: Paul says salvation is by grace through faith and is God's gift; set beside the commentary's list of belief and righteous deeds, this frames the ground of rescue differently.

basis: Not from works, so no one may boast
note: Paul explicitly denies that salvation is from works, while the commentary includes righteous deeds in the description of those outside loss; the contrast concerns how deeds relate to rescue.

basis: Speak truth each with the neighbor
note: Paul commands each person to put away falsehood and speak truth with the neighbor because they belong to one another; this is a direct communal truth-speaking analogue to the commentary's mutual counsel.
The surah makes patience and counsel reciprocal under human loss; Paul tells believers to carry one another's burdens, giving shared weight a practical communal answer.

basis: Persistence in doing good and harvest in due season
note: Paul urges doing good without weariness because a harvest comes in due time if one does not give up; this joins the commentary's righteous action and patience to an agricultural yield.

basis: Stirring one another to love and good works
note: The addressees are told to provoke one another toward love and good works; this closely matches the commentary's reciprocal counsel and righteous deeds, though it specifies love rather than truth.
The surah names good deeds and reciprocal counsel; Hebrews calls hearers to consider how to stir one another to love and good works, supplying a concrete communal form for the surah's linked actions.
The assembly is to encourage one another as the day approaches; this supplies the reciprocal communal action behind the commentary's repeated mutual exhortation.

basis: encouraging one another as the day nears
note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel is urgent under human loss; Hebrews asks the assembly not to abandon meeting and to encourage one another increasingly as the day approaches, adding persistence in a gathered community to the preceding call to good works.
The commentary joins righteous deeds to mutual counsel in patience; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will to receive what was promised, linking conduct and sustained waiting.

basis: Painful discipline later yields peaceful fruit
note: Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit; this gives a precise interpretive bridge to the commentary's bitter medicine, whose discomfort is paired with healing benefit.
The commentary's bitter remedy comes out of pressure and heals; Hebrews calls discipline painful in the present but says it later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.

The commentary calls patience a bitter but beneficial outcome of pressure; Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him, giving a particular sufferer's ordeal and later good beside the discipline image in 12:11.
The community must exhort one another daily so no one is hardened by sin's deceit; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel a concrete protective purpose against moral loss.

basis: Faith and patience inherit the promises
note: The author urges imitation of those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this directly pairs two qualities named in the commentary's saved group.

basis: Enduring trial leads to the crown of life
note: James calls blessed the person who endures trial and promises the crown of life; this connects patience under pressure to a salvific outcome.
James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this gives the commentary's bitter, pressed sabr an explicit formation process under trial.
The commentary places sabr after the human's pressured loss; James says testing faith produces endurance, stating the productive sequence behind the commentary's pressed remedy.
James says endurance must have its full effect so people become complete; this interprets patience as a formed quality with a beneficial end, like the commentary's medicine metaphor.

The commentary connects sabr to overcoming khusr as diminution; James asks that endurance complete its work so the faithful become complete and lack nothing, joining endurance to the reversal of lack.
James asks whether a person who claims faith but has no works can be saved; this directly tests the commentary's pairing of belief and righteous action, making their relation explicit.
James says faith without works is dead; this gives a specific Christian account of why belief and deeds belong together in the commentary's exception from loss.

The commentary calls sabr a bitter but healing result of pressure; James recalls Job's endurance and the Lord's compassionate outcome, locating patience within a particular sufferer's eventual relief.

basis: Turning a wanderer back from truth
note: James addresses fellow believers and says that whoever turns a brother back from wandering from the truth performs a communal corrective act like the commentary's mutual counsel in truth.
James adds that bringing the wanderer back saves that person's soul from death; this makes the truth-directed mutual correction a rescue from loss, not merely instruction.

basis: The farmer patiently waits for precious fruit
note: James tells the community to wait patiently like a farmer for the earth's precious crop; it links patience to delayed yield, though the image is cultivation rather than extraction.

The commentary places patience after pressed produce and scarcity; James asks the community to wait like a farmer for the precious fruit of the earth through its early and late rains, joining endurance, water and eventual yield.

basis: Pruning a fruitful branch for more fruit
note: Jesus says the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so it bears more fruit; this gives the commentary's grape and pressure images a contrasting cultivation model where cutting increases future yield.

The commentary imagines something removed under pressure so that good can emerge; Jesus says the Father prunes a fruit-bearing branch to make it bear more fruit, joining painful subtraction to a larger yield.
At the crucifixion Jesus says he thirsts; this is a specific bodily thirst scene beside the commentary's dried tongue, with the speaker's impending death making the need unresolved.
The commentary's dried tongue belongs to one under pressure; at the cross Jesus says he is thirsty, bringing bodily thirst into an account of sustained suffering.

basis: Sour wine lifted to the thirsty Jesus
note: The bystanders raise sour wine to Jesus after he says he thirsts; the drink is acidic relief in a death scene, not the beneficial bitter remedy described in the commentary.
The commentary's liquid can be bitter rather than simply refreshing; at the cross sour wine is lifted to the thirsty Jesus on a sponge, coupling distress with an acrid drink rather than plain water.

basis: drink that ends thirst and becomes a spring
note: The commentary links a dry tongue, a relieving drink and a valuable liquid kept within; Jesus says the water he gives ends thirst and becomes a spring within the recipient, turning received relief into a continuing source.
The commentary's dry tongue requires a life-giving drink; Jesus calls anyone thirsty to come to him and drink, offering spiritual relief through the bodily action named in the scene.

The commentary's beneficial extract becomes an outflow to others; Jesus says living water will flow from the believer's inner being, turning received drink into a source rather than a private possession.
The commentary names a thirst-dried tongue and liquid that could relieve distress; the rich man in torment asks for a fingertip of water to cool his tongue, but the relief he requests is withheld.
The commentary's middle human is in loss and its close calls for sabr; Jesus tells persecuted hearers they will gain their lives through endurance, directly reversing threatened loss.

basis: Losing life for Jesus saves it
note: Jesus says the one who loses life for his sake will save it; this reverses the commentary's general human loss into a paradoxical self-loss that leads to rescue.

The commentary joins a valuable extract, its vessel and generous outflow; the woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly nard and pours its contents on Jesus, making the opened container the condition of the gift.

basis: cup of suffering and yielded will
note: The commentary makes a cup and its difficult contents part of the pressured person's response; Jesus asks that the cup pass from him but submits to the Father's will, using the vessel for an ordeal faced with endurance.

basis: Wine mixed with myrrh is refused
note: Mark says wine mixed with myrrh is offered to Jesus and he does not take it; the plant resin in a wine drink recalls the commentary's plant-derived bitter essence, though Mark does not call it bitter or medicinal.

Jesus says new wine put into old wineskins bursts them and both wine and skins are lost; unlike the commentary's corked bottle retaining a medicinal essence, this vessel fails under pressure and causes loss.

basis: cup of water given to a disciple
note: The commentary says expressed goodness can take the form of a gift; Jesus promises a reward for giving even a cup of water because the recipient belongs to Christ, measuring charity by a concrete drink.
The commentary's final sabr answers the human's peril of loss; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved in a discourse about affliction and betrayal.
The commentary makes liquid relief an act of goodness; the king identifies himself with a thirsty person to whom the righteous gave drink, tying a small bodily gift to the judgment of good action.

basis: fruit of vine deferred until kingdom
note: The commentary recalls renewed pressing after a time of deprivation; Jesus says he will not drink the fruit of the vine again until drinking it new with the disciples in his Father's kingdom, setting present abstention beside future shared wine.

basis: Jesus asks that the cup pass, then submits
note: Jesus asks whether the cup can pass but submits to the Father's will; the cup makes suffering a drink-like burden, while the scene adds willing endurance rather than the commentary's extracted medicine.

basis: Jesus accepts the cup he must drink
note: Jesus says that if the cup cannot pass unless he drinks it, the Father's will be done; this continuation turns the cup from a requested escape into accepted suffering.

basis: Wine mixed with gall is offered and refused
note: Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting; this gives a specific bitter drink in a suffering scene, but the text presents no healing benefit like the commentary's medicine.

basis: wine mixed with gall offered and refused
note: The commentary's drink can be a bitter product amid suffering; before crucifixion Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting, so an acrid cup accompanies pressure without becoming the healing drink the commentary imagines.

The commentary's stopper and vessel keep the pressed essence from loss; Jesus' wineskin saying says old skins burst under new wine so the wine spills, whereas suitable skins preserve both wine and vessel.

basis: poured offering joined to others' faith
note: The commentary's pressured essence is given away; Paul depicts himself as poured out upon the community's sacrificial service of faith, though the passage supplies neither a pressed plant nor a sealed container.

basis: Sweet taste turns bitter after eating
note: John reports that the scroll tasted sweet and then made his stomach bitter; this locates bitterness after ingestion, unlike the commentary's bitter extract whose bitterness is already the medicinal quality.

basis: Scroll sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
note: John is told to eat the scroll, which will be sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach; the two-stage taste gives the commentary's swallowed bitter medicine a distinct prophetic counterpart.

basis: Saints' endurance, God's commands, and faith in Jesus
note: The verse defines the saints by endurance, keeping God's commands, and faith in Jesus; this closely gathers patience, faithful action, and belief in the kind of people the commentary exempts from loss.

basis: Earth's grapes thrown into the winepress of wrath
note: The angel gathers the earth's grapes and throws them into God's great winepress; this directly turns the commentary's pressing that yields good essence into an apocalyptic harvest of wrath.

The commentary's press can yield goodness for people; Revelation has an angel gather the earth's grape harvest into the great winepress of divine wrath, giving the same extraction scene a punitive end.
The press is trodden outside the city and blood flows from it; this specifies the destructive yield of the preceding winepress, in contrast to the commentary's useful extracted juice.

basis: blood flows from the trodden press
note: The commentary treats the outflow from pressing as a possible valuable essence; Revelation's next verse says blood flows from the winepress after it is trodden, specifying a violent extract rather than a remedy.
The commentary links a treasured liquid with giving and thirst; Revelation invites the thirsty to take the water of life without payment, making the valuable drink an unrestricted gift.

basis: Wormwood makes waters bitter and kills many
note: The star named Wormwood makes the waters bitter and many die from them; this directly reverses the commentary's bitter plant extract as medicine by making bitter liquid lethal.
The commentary calls the bitter extract a medicine; Revelation says waters made bitter by Wormwood kill many drinkers, a concrete reversal in which bitter liquid is harmful rather than curative.

basis: food and drink given to an enemy
note: The commentary interprets beneficial liquid as generosity under pressure; Paul repeats the instruction to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy drink, carrying the concrete act from Proverbs into counsel to a Christian community.

basis: good overcomes evil after water gift
note: The commentary says a squeezed essence can become goodness given away; after directing food and drink to an enemy in 12:20, Paul says to overcome evil with good, naming the moral effect of that costly gift.

basis: Perseverance in doing good leads to eternal life
note: Paul describes those who persist in doing good and seek glory and immortality as receiving eternal life; this combines the commentary's good action and patience in a salvific outcome.

Paul contrasts those who obey truth with those who disobey truth and pursue unrighteousness, who receive wrath; this counters the commentary's mutual truth-counsel by depicting refusal of truth as a path to judgment.
Paul says affliction produces endurance, which gives the commentary's squeezed, bitter sabr a developmental reading: pressure can generate the quality that sustains a person.
The commentary's pressure can issue in sabr rather than mere loss; Paul says tribulation produces endurance, making affliction the occasion for the saving quality named at the surah's end.

basis: Endurance produces tested character and hope
note: Paul says endurance produces tested character and hope; this continues the commentary's image of a beneficial quality formed through pressure.

Paul says God's love has been poured into believers' hearts; the commentary specifically notes Qur'anic patience poured over people, and this supplies a Christian liquid metaphor for an inward virtue, while naming love rather than patience.

The commentary develops sabr as something poured over threatened people; in Paul's sequence after tribulation and endurance, God's love is poured into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit, giving a distinct beneficial liquid image to what follows pressure.

The commentary calls the sap named sabr a bitter medicine; this mandate presents patience as sweet and valuable in moral struggle, offering a contrary taste for the virtue. The precise subsection within Mandate 5.1 needs verification.

The commentary describes a bitter medicine produced by pressure; the rabbinic teaching says Torah, the land of Israel and the world to come are granted through suffering, interpreting pain as a passage to valuable goods.

The commentary proposes a healing value in painful pressure; a sage in the discussion of afflictions says he wants neither the sufferings nor their reward, preserving a dissenting response to the claim that pain is worth its yield.

The commentary's pressure produces a useful, bitter essence; the rabbinic reading of Israel as an olive tree says the olive gives oil only when beaten and Israel turns toward the good through affliction, making the extraction a moral process.

basis: Maror eaten to recall Egyptian oppression
note: At the Passover meal bitter herbs are part of the narrated memory of bondage; this makes bitterness a communal ritual of remembered suffering, unlike the commentary's bitter remedy.

The commentary distinguishes valuable contents from the container and diminished exterior; Avot says to inspect what a jar holds, since a new jar may contain old wine and an old jar may contain none, making contents the measure of worth.

basis: reward according to effort and pain
note: The commentary proposes that a painful process can produce a valuable good; the maxim associates reward with the labor or pain expended, providing a Jewish ethical reading of effort's yield without claiming literal grape pressing.

basis: Accept what comes and be patient in humiliation
note: Sirach tells the reader to accept what comes and be patient in humiliation; it links patience to receiving painful experience, an explicit bridge to the commentary's bitter remedy.

basis: Gold tested in fire; acceptable people in humiliation
note: Sirach compares tested people to gold in a furnace; it supplies a refining image in which affliction tests and qualifies, alongside the commentary's pressure that produces bitter sabr.

Sirach says the Lord made medicines from the earth and a sensible person does not reject them; it supplies a Jewish wisdom frame for the commentary's medicinal plant exudate as a beneficial natural substance.

basis: Colleagues sharpen one another in Torah
note: The Talmud applies iron sharpening iron to scholars who sharpen one another in Torah; this interprets mutual counsel as reciprocal learning and correction, a specific Jewish account of the commentary's tawāṣī relation.

The commentary values the held essence and the vessel that protects it; the rabbinic exchange about fine wine in earthen jars uses the vessel to explain why wisdom is preserved with humility, transferring storage to a human quality.
Tobit's father regains sight after fish gall is applied; this is a concrete natural-substance cure alongside the commentary's medicinal tree exudate, though its source is animal rather than plant.

basis: Jar of meal and jug of oil do not fail during drought
note: Elijah promises that the widow's jar and jug will not be emptied until rain returns; the contained provision in scarcity parallels the commentary's stored essence and its Yusuf scene of relief after famine.

basis: The jar and jug remain supplied
note: The narrative says the widow's jar and jug did not fail as promised; this continuation shows stored liquid and food sustaining life through drought, unlike a one-time extracted dose.

basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence
note: The commentary's dry mouth asks how pressure can end in liquid relief; Solomon's prayer envisages the heavens being restrained from rain and the people seeking forgiveness so water may return.

The commentary treats a saving quality as poured onto the pressured person; Hannah explains that she has poured out her soul before the Lord amid deep distress, an inward liquid image for responding to affliction.

basis: Fig cake applied to a boil; recovery
note: Isaiah orders a fig cake laid on Hezekiah's boil and Hezekiah recovers; this gives a concrete plant-based remedy alongside the commentary's bitter tree extract called medicine.

The commentary's bitter extract is a medicine; Elisha adds flour to the pot after the prophets fear death in the stew, and the food becomes harmless. The bridge is a healing substance in a vessel, though the passage does not call the flour bitter or describe squeezing it.

basis: Oil fills every borrowed vessel and then stops
note: The widow's oil keeps filling containers until there is no vessel left, when the flow stops; it gives a precise parallel to liquid collected and held by a vessel, with provision released rather than a corked medicine.

basis: Treader of grapes overtaken by the sower; hills drip wine
note: Amos pictures restoration so abundant that grape-treading overlaps sowing and mountains drip sweet wine; this makes pressing the sign of relief and plenty, as in the commentary's post-scarcity year.
The commentary's post-scarcity year is marked by pressing again; Amos pictures restored abundance so great that the mountains drip wine and the hills flow with it.

basis: خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, table sound correspondence
note: The commentary calls human khusr a diminution; Daniel's verdict says the king has been weighed and found lacking, making deficiency a judgment on a person rather than only a reduced quantity.

basis: Commentary label root ء ن س; Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence only and unverified
note: Daniel sees one like a bar enash, a humanlike figure who receives dominion; this contrasts the commentary's collective humanity with a singular exalted use of the related Aramaic word.

basis: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence
note: The commentary's al-insan is exposed to loss; Daniel sees one like a human being coming with heaven's clouds before the Ancient of Days, using the Aramaic cognate for a humanlike figure poised for a different outcome.

The commentary's human stands under the sentence of loss; the figure described as humanlike in 7:13 receives lasting dominion and a kingdom here, completing that scene with an opposite destiny. The Aramaic אנש occurs in the preceding verse.

basis: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
note: The Hebrew verb עצר closes the heavens so rain and yield cease; this restraint is the agricultural inverse of the commentary's squeezing that releases juice and, in its Yusuf comparison, marks relief after scarcity.

basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence
note: The commentary's pressure and dry tongue are tied to withholding liquid; Deuteronomy warns that God may shut the heavens so no rain falls, using עצר for held-back water that brings loss of the land's produce.

basis: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
note: Moses says Israel lacked nothing during the wilderness years; the cognate sense of lack gives a direct counter-reading to the commentary's human placed in decrease and loss.

The commentary calls the expressed sabr an unpleasant medicine; after thirst in the wilderness Israel finds water at Marah but cannot drink it because it is bitter, so the desired liquid initially fails to relieve need.

basis: Marah's bitter water and the wood
note: At Marah the people cannot drink bitter water until Moses throws a tree into it and it becomes sweet; this reverses the commentary's bitter tree extract, which remains bitter yet is named medicine.
The commentary moves from an acrid extract to healing relief; Moses is shown a tree to put into Marah's bitter water, and the water becomes drinkable through an intervention within the liquid itself.

After the bitter-water episode, YHWH identifies himself as Israel's healer; this makes explicit the healing frame that the commentary gives to bitter sabr, though the remedy and bitterness work differently.
The commentary calls the bitter extract a medicine; after making Marah's water drinkable, God names himself Israel's healer, making the preceding unpleasant-water episode a setting for healing.

basis: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
note: Abraham asks whether five righteous people might be lacking from fifty; the Hebrew cognate makes decrease numerical and ties the missing count to whether a city is spared.

basis: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
note: The Hebrew form עצר says YHWH had closed every womb in Abimelech's house; this related closure gives a bodily analogue to the commentary's stopper sealing a vessel, with withheld fertility instead of preserved medicine.

basis: Commentary's 12:36 prison dream; grapes pressed into a cup
note: The imprisoned cupbearer dreams of taking grapes and pressing them into Pharaoh's cup, giving the commentary's prison grape-press scene in its own narrative setting.
The commentary recalls the prisoner's dream of squeezing grapes; in Joseph's prison the cupbearer presses the grapes into Pharaoh's cup, joining confinement, extracted drink and service in one scene.

The commentary reads pressing after hardship as a sign of relief; Joseph interprets the cupbearer's pressing dream as restoration to his former office in three days, while the cupbearer rather than Joseph receives this immediate relief.

basis: Seven years of famine after seven years of plenty
note: Joseph's dream interpretation predicts seven lean years after abundance; it parallels the commentary's sequence of scarcity and eventual relief while preserving a different order from its pressing year.
The commentary joins post-famine pressing to preserving the extracted good; Joseph orders grain stored under Pharaoh during the good years so that produce can outlast the scarcity ahead.

basis: stored food prevents death in famine
note: The commentary connects the return of pressing after lean years with keeping valuable produce; Joseph says the stored food will sustain Egypt through seven famine years so the land will not perish, stating the life-saving purpose of the storage ordered in the preceding verse.

basis: Commentary label root ص ب ر; Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence only
note: The Hebrew verb צבר describes Joseph piling up grain beyond measure; beside the commentary's corked bottle retaining squeezed essence, the narrow connection is accumulation and storage, not a shared sense of patience.

basis: ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence
note: The commentary's sabr root names the bitter extract and the stopper that keeps it; Genesis says Joseph heaped up grain beyond counting before famine, using צבר for a different act of gathering and preserving what pressure will make valuable.
When famine covers the land, Joseph opens the storehouses; this connects the commentary's retained essence in a closed bottle with stored provision later released to sustain people.

The commentary's pressed and stored good becomes relief when want arrives; as famine spreads, Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain to Egyptians, bringing the preserved supply into use rather than leaving it sealed away.

basis: evil converted into preservation of life
note: The commentary imagines pressure on a person yielding a good that others receive; Joseph tells his brothers that the evil they intended against him was turned toward preserving many lives, interpreting the outcome of his imprisonment and food administration.

The commentary makes renewed pressing a sign that scarcity has ended; Isaiah's judgment removes joy from the vineyards and silences the treader in the winepress, so the same action's absence signals loss.

basis: Tongue fails for thirst; water is promised
note: The needy have no water and their tongue fails from thirst; this closely matches the commentary's dried tongue, while Isaiah's promised springs reverse depletion with relief.
The commentary's pressed, dry tongue needs liquid relief; Isaiah describes needy people seeking water with none available and tongues parched with thirst, before God's promise to answer them.

basis: A winepress prepared for grapes but wild grapes produced
note: The vineyard owner builds a winepress expecting good grapes but finds wild grapes; the image makes the commentary's generous essence contingent on a yield that can instead disappoint.

The commentary expects good essence from pressing; Isaiah's vineyard owner prepares a winepress but gets bad grapes from carefully tended vines, reversing the hoped-for product before the vineyard's judgment.

The commentary gives the pressed extract a moral sense of goodness; Isaiah explains his vineyard's failed fruit as Israel's failure to yield justice and righteousness, clarifying why a harvest image can judge a human community.

The commentary turns expressed essence into generosity; Isaiah asks a person to give of himself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted, after which light rises from darkness, connecting costly giving to relief.

The commentary's dried tongue and beneficial outflow invite a restoration image; Isaiah promises guidance and satisfaction in parched places until the person is like a watered garden and unfailing spring.

basis: Winepress trodden in wrath; blood on garments
note: The divine speaker treads the press in anger and blood stains his clothing, a direct counter-image to the commentary's extracted juice as good and generous giving.
The commentary's pressing produces a potentially healing good; Isaiah's solitary winepress treader makes red garments an image of wrath against peoples, a specific contrary use of the same action.

The commentary makes the juice pressed from grapes an image of good that should be kept; Isaiah says a cluster containing new wine must not be destroyed because a blessing is in it, then applies that preservation to God's servants.
The commentary ends with a sealed bottle that retains its medicinal essence, whereas Jeremiah's chosen cisterns are cracked and cannot hold water, making failed containment a charge against Judah.

basis: broken cisterns unable to hold water
note: The commentary's vessel keeps its valuable liquid from loss; Jeremiah contrasts the living-water source with cracked cisterns that cannot hold water, making a failed container an image of a people's self-inflicted deprivation.

The commentary's stopper and vessel keep something valuable for later; Jeremiah orders purchase documents put in an earthenware jar so they survive many days during Jerusalem's siege, preserving a sign of future restoration.

basis: Wine left on its lees and not poured between vessels
note: Moab's undisturbed wine retains its flavor because it has not been poured from vessel to vessel; the commentary's cork likewise preserves a liquid, but Jeremiah makes stillness a figure for complacency.
The commentary's human stands in diminishment between pressure and relief; Job says a person born of woman has few days and is full of trouble, sharpening the vulnerability of the one being pressed.

basis: Wine with no vent; new wineskins ready to burst
note: The commentary's cork holds squeezed liquid in a bottle; Elihu instead likens unspoken words to fermenting wine with no vent, so the same containment intensifies pressure toward rupture.

basis: Commentary label root ء ن س; Hebrew אנש, regular sound correspondence and BDB Arabic-cognate note
note: Job asks what אנוש, a mortal human, is that God gives him such attention; it lends the commentary's generic human between pressure and loss a specific mortal and vulnerable register.

basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB cognate note
